name: Emeka Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Emeka, and thanks for your time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really believe. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mr Whitlock at Old Mill Farm, a hundred and twenty beef cattle and about two hundred acres of wheat and oats. I'm there by six, feeding the cattle in the yard, bedding them with straw, then fencing or carting grain or whatever needs doing. Mr Whitlock is seventy and a widower, so I do more of the heavy work every year. I've been there two and a half years and I'm still learning his ways.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value in it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I value honest work, and I value that Mr Whitlock trusts me with his animals. My father had a smallholding and lost it to debt when I was twelve, so working land again means something to me. What's hard is the money. Grace and I are getting married at our church next June, and the wedding fund and three months of savings are all we have.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I don't need a machine to tell me a cow is lame. Grace uses her phone for everything, and that's her business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. A machine was never going to replace a man who gets up at five. I'd say that after church and to the lads at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries stay the same, and they're not about computers. Mr Whitlock is seventy and has no children, and nobody knows what happens to Old Mill when he stops. If the big estate next door buys Old Mill, they'll run it with their own men and their GPS tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and keep showing Mr Whitlock I can be trusted with more. Grace and I would keep putting three hundred a month into the wedding fund. I'd ask Mr Whitlock straight, one evening, what his plans are for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like life. Not easy, but familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope Mr Whitlock says, when you ask him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hope he says he'd rent the land to me when he retires, even a part of it. It's what an older farmer used to do for a young man who worked for him. I don't know if people do that anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the estate buys Old Mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be one more worker on a big farm, if they want me, which they might not. The estate manager has never said hello to me. That would hurt more than any robot.

say: A machine was never going to replace **a man who works**.
I'd say **I told you so** after church and at the market.
think: My worries are about **Mr Whitlock's age**, not computers.
Nobody knows what happens to **Old Mill** when he stops.
The **big estate** next door might buy it and use their own men.
do: Keep showing Mr Whitlock I can be **trusted** with more.
Put **three hundred a month** into the wedding fund.
Ask Mr Whitlock straight about his **plans for the farm**.
feel: **Familiar**: not easy, but the life I know.
S0.quote: If the big estate next door buys Old Mill, they'll run it with their own men and their GPS tractors.
fieldNote: His unease is about **succession at Old Mill**, not AI.
He hopes for a **tenancy** from Mr Whitlock, an old-style arrangement.
His father's **lost smallholding** shapes how much the land matters.

steps.text: Keep feeding and bedding the Old Mill cattle as now
Put three hundred a month into the wedding fund with Grace

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say these companies sell change because change makes them money, and families pay for it. At church I'd say we look after each other, like we always have. I don't go on the internet to argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the office side doesn't touch me, because Mr Whitlock does his paperwork in a ledger and I don't do any. But Grace works the counter at the chemist, and if the AI answers questions and books things, her hours could go. And the big estate next door would get even cheaper with all this, which makes it more likely they buy Old Mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. We'd cut the wedding back, maybe sixty guests instead of a hundred, and put the difference into savings. I'm not going on any computer course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my own hands, more for the farm and for Grace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would cutting the wedding be hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Grace's mother, very. She has a list of cousins as long as my arm. But I'd rather start married life with savings than with a big party and an empty account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the estate would get cheaper. Who would you blame if they bought Old Mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, for paying grants to the biggest farms, and the estate's owners in the city. Not Mr Whitlock. A man has a right to sell his land, but the game is tilted.

say: These companies sell **change** because it makes them **money**.
At church I'd say we **look after each other**.
think: The **office side** doesn't touch me; Mr Whitlock uses a ledger.
**Grace's hours** at the chemist could go if AI answers customers.
The **big estate** would get cheaper and more likely to buy Old Mill.
do: Keep doing the **farm work** the same way.
Cut the wedding to **sixty guests** and save the difference.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the farm and **Grace** than my hands.
S1.quote: I'd rather start married life with savings than with a big party and an empty account.
fieldNote: He sees desk changes hitting **Grace's counter job**, not his.
He blames **grants and city owners**, while defending Mr Whitlock's right to sell.
He'd **shrink the wedding** rather than learn new tools.

steps.text: Keep working the cattle and grain at Old Mill
Cut the June wedding from a hundred guests to sixty
Put the wedding savings difference into the joint account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing God, and we'll pay for it. I'd say families and churches will have to carry each other, because the government won't manage it. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect family farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me. In 2028 the AI takes Grace's counter job and every office round here. Around 2031 the robots can feed cattle and drive a combine, and I'd be thirty-one, married, maybe with a baby, and nothing to sell but my back. Mr Whitlock would sell to the estate, and the estate would buy robots, not men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry in June, but in the church hall with sandwiches. We'd move in with Grace's parents for two years to save rent. I'd ask Pastor Daniel and the men at church who has work, any work. And I'd vote and talk for anyone who'll stop big companies buying up farms with public money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground has been sold from under me, again. Like my father's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'again'. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I was twelve, a man in a suit came to my father's kitchen and the farm was gone by Christmas. My father never worked land again. I swore I'd get back on it, and now a robot might take it instead of a bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Living with Grace's parents after the wedding. How would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard on my pride. A man should give his wife her own home. But family is there for times like this, and her father is a kind man.

say: This is people **playing God**, and we'll pay for it.
**Families and churches** will have to carry each other.
I'd vote for whoever **protects family farms**.
think: In **2028** AI takes Grace's counter job.
Around **2031** robots feed cattle and drive combines.
Mr Whitlock would sell, and the estate buys **robots, not men**.
do: Marry in June in the **church hall** with sandwiches.
Move in with **Grace's parents** for two years.

feel: Like the **ground** has been sold from under me **again**.
S2.quote: When I was twelve, a man in a suit came to my father's kitchen and the farm was gone by Christmas.
fieldNote: He sees **Grace's job** going in 2028 and his own around 2031.
The scenario reopens his **father's lost farm**, a deep wound.

He'd **vote** for protecting family farms, the one political act he names.

steps.text: Hold the June wedding in the church hall with sandwiches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to prepare, and they should, without waiting for help. I'd say it at church and at the young farmers' club. Hard work and each other, that's what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just with more years of wages first. Grace's job goes around 2031, and the robots come around 2034, when I'm thirty-five. If Mr Whitlock let me rent part of Old Mill before then, I'd at least have land in my name. But I'd be competing with an estate full of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry as planned and save hard, four hundred a month once we're married. I'd ask Mr Whitlock this winter about renting the forty acres by the river. And I'd join the family farmers' association, because together we can push for small tenancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but with something to hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you farm forty acres without robots, if the estate has them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grass-fed beef, sold to people who care where it came from. Forty acres of grass-fed beef won't make me rich, but it might keep Grace and me fed and keep me on land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never touch a computer. Would you sell beef online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace would. She's better at that than me, and I'm not too proud to let my wife do what she's good at. I'd do the cattle.

Hard work and **each other** are what we have.
think: It's the **same ending**, with more years of wages first.
Grace's job goes around **2031**; robots come around **2034**.

fieldNote: Five years gives him room to chase a **small tenancy**.

steps.text: Save four hundred a month after the June wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and a man who works hard can prepare for nearly anything in ten years. I'd tell the young farmers' club to get land if they can, and to look after their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel more settled. The AI comes in 2036 and the robots around 2039, when I'd be thirty-nine. If I can get the river acres and build a herd, I'd have ten years to make a name. Robots might come, but people will still want beef from a farmer they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Grace in June as planned. I'd ask Mr Whitlock this winter about renting the river acres, and buy twenty store cattle with our savings over two years. We'd plan for children, and I'd keep working for Mr Whitlock as long as he needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. There's still a shadow at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the shadow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day a robot can do everything I do, cheaper. In 2039 I'd have children at school. I pray I'm wrong about how fast it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say get the land, and never borrow more than you can pay back. He learned that the hard way. I'd listen.

Young farmers should **get land** and look after their families.
think: I'd feel more **settled**, with robots around **2039**.
With the river acres I'd have **ten years** to make a name.
People will still want beef from a **farmer they know**.

S4.quote: My father would say get the land, and never borrow more than you can pay back.

steps.text: Marry Grace in June and plan for children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Grace and I would be starting a family with no work and no land. What would help is starter tenancies for young farmers, and an end to grants that only help the biggest estates. Apprenticeships, not handouts, so a young man can learn a trade properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When you can't control what happens, you need something that holds you steady. For me that's God, my wife and my work, in that order.

headlineQuote: When you can't control what happens, you need something that holds you steady.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** farm worker at **Old Mill Farm**, working for a widowed farmer of seventy.
His father **lost a smallholding** to debt, so getting back on land means everything to him.
He's marrying **Grace** in June, never uses AI, and leans on **church and family**.
Fast AGI leaves him **alarmed**; with time he hopes to rent land and raise beef.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, starting a family with no work and no **land**.
whatWouldHelp: **Starter tenancies** for young farmers and fairer **grants**.
